newsitem.title: INDIA: India's Punjab seals borders ahead of local polls.
newsitem.headline: India's Punjab seals borders ahead of local polls.

text.p: Indian security forces sealed off Punjab province's borders with Pakistan and neighbouring states on Wednesday ahead of key assembly polls in a region recovering from years of separatist violence.

Police officials said Punjab's borders with the Indian states of Rajasthan and Jammu and Kashmir were being closely monitored to prevent the incursion of any militants ahead of the state elections set for Friday.
"Punjab's border with Pakistan is better manned than what we can say of Rajasthan and Kashmir," Varinder Pal Singh, a senior police official in the border city of Amritsar, told Reuters.
"We have sealed off the entry points so that nobody sneaks in to create trouble on election day," he said. Local officials said more than 100,000 police were deployed across the state.
Peace has largely returned to the fertile region since a decade-long separatist revolt began to wane in the early 1990s.
Friday's assembly elections to 117 seats were the first polls in nearly two decades not overshadowed by Sikh separatists fighting for a separate homeland called Khalistan, or Land of the Pure.
"The battle of the bullets is over," proclaimed a campaigner. "Punjab has now decided irrevocably to seek the way of the ballot to decide its future."
The elections were regarded as a crucial phase in the state's move towards peace.
"These elections will see a very high turnout, maybe 60 to 65 percent," said Singh.
The resurgent Akali Dal party, which sat out the last state polls in 1992, was widely expected to emerge as the winner, displacing the Congress party which has ruled for five years.

"The Congress has been in bad odour among the Sikhs ever since the army assault on the Golden Temple," said a retired Sikh police official, speaking outside Amritsar's glistening Golden Temple, Sikhdom's holiest shrine.
He was referring to a clash in 1984 between Sikh militants holed up in the temple and Indian troops who flushed them out.
The battle destroyed large parts of the shrine. The assault is widely considered the trigger for the Sikh separatist uprising in which more than 20,000 people were killed.
But most people now agree that militancy has been quelled.
The temple's dome glistened under a balmy sun in Amritsar on Wednesday, many of its two million inhabitants looking surer than ever in two decades about peace returning to the region.
Sikh volunteers have been working feverishly for several weeks to change the 150-year-old gold plating of the ancient shrine. In a few days 600 kg (1,320 lb) of new gold plates will adorn the temple.
"The temple's new shine may well resemble a new hope in Punjab," said Amarjit Singh, an official at the Golden Temple and a witness to the 1984 clash between militants and soldiers.

The polls have seen a host of strange bedfellows. The right-wing Hindu nationalist Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) has joined hands with the Akali Dal, accused by the Congress of fanning Sikh separatism.
